hero.headline: Western St. Lucie County flooding prompts emergency meeting, push for faster study
hero.teaser: The North St. Lucie River Water Control District held an emergency meeting Monday after last week’s flooding submerged homes, farms and roads in western St. Lucie County. Later Mon
hero.body:
The North St. Lucie River Water Control District held an emergency meeting Monday after last week’s flooding submerged homes, farms and roads in western St. Lucie County. Later Monday, Port St. Lucie Councilman David Pickett urged the city to accelerate a stormwater study planned for 2029.

 Farmers, residents and representatives of Save the Chimps attended the district meeting to seek answers and long-term drainage solutions. District President Steve Cassens said the existing system has limits during extreme rainfall. “We can manage water maybe 3, 4, 5, 6 inches. We can’t manage water in the quantities that we got.” District officials discussed examining engineering options as part of a possible long-range plan.

 They also addressed waterway and ditch maintenance, including concerns about a creek in Western Fort Pierce that serves as a primary drainage route. The district said it systematically cleans ditches within its boundaries.

 At Monday’s Port St. Lucie City Council meeting, Pickett said he had sent two memos to the city manager addressing floodwaters and wanted the stormwater study expedited rather than waiting until 2029. He also raised concerns about flooding in Tradition and called for examining stormwater systems before distributing certain stormwater fees to community development districts.

 Justin Akerley, who helps operate Saint Lucie Farm Preserve in west Fort Pierce, attended both meetings. He told council members he believes continued development is adding pressure to drainage infrastructure and urged city leaders to reconsider development’s effects on flooding. “I’ve got friends that have calves dying that are flooded, they can’t get out,” he said. “It’s a terrible, terrible situation for everybody.

 There’s people that have lost their homes.” Akerley and Michael Hale operate the working agritourism farm, which produces hay, cut flowers, beef and assorted vegetables. The farm also hosts community agricultural events.

 Conditions had significantly improved at Save the Chimps, a sanctuary in western St. Lucie County where staff used drones to deliver food to chimpanzees while several roads were underwater. “A short 40 hours after that, we’re almost completely dry on our roads,” Mark Yohannan said. Residents and farmers at Monday’s district meeting sought ways to reduce the risk of similar flooding during another extreme rainfall event.

cards.headline: Martin County commissioners to review safety requirements for train quiet zones
cards.teaser: A 10:30 a.m. presentation Tuesday will examine potential quiet-zone benefits, risks and crossing improvements following continued pressure from residents.
cards.body:
Martin County commissioners are scheduled to review safety requirements and potential improvements Tuesday morning for proposed railroad quiet zones, which would end routine train horn requirements at designated crossings. The review follows continued pressure from residents seeking relief from train noise along the Florida East Coast Railway.

 Public Works staff is scheduled to present an update at 10:30 a.m. on the Railroad Safety Capital Improvement Program and the county’s evaluation of establishing one or more quiet zones. The presentation will outline potential risks and benefits, along with the safety requirements and improvements needed to establish the zones. Commissioners are expected to discuss the findings and give staff direction on how to proceed.

 Crossings would have to meet federal safety requirements before quiet zones could be established. Train engineers would retain the ability to sound their horns when necessary for safety. Hobe Sound resident Glenn Malone supports reducing horn noise while preserving engineers’ ability to use the horn for safety. Another Hobe Sound resident, Jeffry Aderman, has raised concerns about train noise throughout the day and night.

 Brightline began commercial operations along the Florida East Coast Railway through the Treasure Coast in September 2023, adding approximately 32 daily train trips through the corridor. The increased rail traffic prompted residents to call on county leaders to explore quiet zones.

 Commissioners decided against pursuing quiet zones at a March 11, 2025, meeting after reviewing options presented by county staff. Following continued resident concerns, they revisited the issue in May 2026 and directed staff to continue evaluating the possibility. Tuesday’s scheduled presentation continues that evaluation.

cards.headline: SUV turned into motorcycle’s path in fatal Indian River County crash, FHP says
cards.teaser: The Florida Highway Patrol says an SUV turned left into the path of a motorcycle during Monday’s fatal crash on 37th Street. The motorcyclist, a 58-year-old man, died at a hospital, and the SUV driver suffered minor injuries.
cards.body:
A crash Monday afternoon on 37th Street in Indian River County initially reported as killing at least one person involved an SUV turning into a motorcycle’s path, according to new details from the Florida Highway Patrol. FHP said the motorcycle’s 58-year-old driver died after being taken to a hospital, while the SUV driver suffered minor injuries.

 The collision occurred around 3:43 p.m. near 1850 37th Street in unincorporated Indian River County. According to FHP, an 82-year-old woman was driving a 2018 Toyota RAV4 east on 37th Street before the crash. She stopped in the roadway while waiting to make a left turn into Indian River MRI.

 The SUV then turned into the path of a westbound 2017 Harley-Davidson motorcycle, and the two vehicles collided, FHP said. The agency’s account provides details about the vehicles involved and their movements before the collision that were not included in the initial report of the fatal crash.

 The motorcycle driver was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where he was pronounced dead. FHP reported that the woman driving the SUV had minor injuries. The initial report had not specified who died or provided information about injuries to the other driver.

 The crash prompted the closure of westbound 37th Street between U.S. Highway 1 and 17th Avenue. The Florida Highway Patrol described its investigation into the fatal collision as active.

cards.headline: Florida's Roof Age Law: The Roof Inspection Treasure Coast Homeowners Can Request Before Replacing a Roof Over 15 Years Old
cards.teaser: Under Florida Statute 627.7011, a homeowner with a roof 15 years or older can have it inspected before an insurer requires replacement. Here is what Martin and St. Lucie County homeowners should know, and what a proper roof inspection documents.
cards.body:
If you own a home in Stuart, Jensen Beach, Palm City, Port St. Lucie, Fort Pierce or anywhere along Hutchinson Island, and your roof is more than 15 years old, there is a good chance you have already received the letter. It says your homeowners insurance will not be renewed unless the roof is replaced. Many Treasure Coast homeowners assume they have two choices: pay for a new roof or lose coverage. Florida law gives them a third option, and most have never heard of it.

 What Florida's Roof Age Law Actually Says

 Florida Statute 627.7011(5), often called the Florida roof age law or the 15-year roof rule, applies to homeowners insurance policies issued or renewed on or after July 1, 2022. For a roof under 15 years old, an insurer may not refuse to issue or renew a policy solely because of the roof's age. For a roof 15 years or older, the insurer must allow the homeowner to have the roof inspected by an authorized inspector, at the homeowner's expense, before requiring replacement as a condition of coverage. If that roof inspection shows the roof has five or more years of remaining useful life, the insurer may not refuse to issue or renew the policy solely because of roof age.

 Authorized inspectors under the statute include Florida-licensed roofing contractors, home inspectors, building code inspectors, general or residential contractors, engineers and architects. The law applies to homeowners policies; it does not apply to a condominium association's master policy, and it does not override every other underwriting decision a carrier is allowed to make. It is a right to be inspected on the roof's actual condition rather than its birthday.

 A plain-language summary of the statute, with the text of the law, is available on our Florida roof age law resource page at mmroofrepair.com/florida-roof-age-law.

 Why Roof Age and Roof Condition Are Not the Same Thing

 On the Treasure Coast, most older homes carry concrete or clay tile roofs. Tile is not the waterproofing layer. The underlayment beneath the tile is.

 A 20- or 25-year-old tile roof can have tile that is largely sound and underlayment that still has service life, with failures concentrated in the places that handle the most water: valleys, perimeter edges, and flashing transitions around chimneys, walls and skylights. Those are the areas that age fastest, because that is where the water goes.

 That is why a documented tile roof inspection so often tells a different story than the installation date. In the more than 100 five-year roof certifications our company has issued since 2023, the deficiencies that put an older tile roof at risk have usually been localized and repairable, not spread evenly across the entire roof. Earlier this year we certified a 25-year-old oceanfront tile roof in Highland Beach that, by age alone, would have been scheduled for a full tear-off.

 The valleys and perimeter edges were rebuilt with new self-adhered underlayment and copper drip edge, each tile went back in its original position, and the roof was certified for more than five years of remaining life with a ten-page photographic record .

 What a Proper Roof Inspection and Five-Year Roof Certification Should Document

 Not every piece of paper called a roof certification is worth the same. A credible five-year roof certification is a licensed professional's written opinion, based on an actual inspection, and it should contain five parts:

 Findings: what the inspector observed across each roof system, including tile, flat sections, underlayment where sampled, flashing and penetrations. Deficiencies identified: active leaks, broken or loose tiles, deteriorated underlayment, damaged sheathing and flashing failures, recorded by location. Repairs performed: exactly what was corrected before the certification was signed. Remaining useful life opinion: the inspector's professional judgment, stated with its basis. Limitations: what was not inspected or tested. A certification is not a warranty, and an honest one says so. Every finding should be tied to dated photographs and the inspector's license number. If a document cannot show you where the problem was found and how it was addressed, it is an opinion without evidence, and it will not hold up when it matters.

 What to Do When the Non-Renewal Letter Arrives

 Read the letter carefully and note the deadline. Most give a defined window to respond. Ask your agent, in writing, whether the non-renewal is based on roof age, and reference Florida Statute 627.7011(5). Schedule a roof inspection with an authorized inspector, and ask up front what the written report will include and whether the inspector photographs every deficiency. If repairs are needed to reach five years of remaining life, have them completed and documented before the certification is signed. Deliver the inspection report and certification to your agent, and keep a copy with your closing documents and your wind mitigation report. Five Questions to Ask Before Signing a Roof Replacement Contract

 Has anyone inspected and photographed the roof's actual condition, or is replacement being recommended by age alone? Where exactly is the roof failing, and is the failure localized to valleys, edges and flashings, or spread across the field? Can the failing sections be rebuilt with new underlayment while the existing tile is preserved and reinstalled? Is the contractor a Florida-licensed roofing contractor, and is the license number on the proposal? Will the contractor return for annual roof inspections so the documentation stays current? When Roof Replacement Is the Right Answer

 This is not an argument against replacing roofs. Some roofs are at the end of their service life. When underlayment has failed across the field, when sheathing is deteriorated in many areas, or when the tile itself is no longer serviceable, replacement is the responsible decision and a good contractor will say so.

 The concern is the roof that gets torn off because of a date on a permit, before anyone has inspected, documented and explained its actual condition. Florida law gives homeowners the right to that inspection. The homeowners who benefit are the ones who know to ask for it.

hero.headline: Martin County commissioners to review safety requirements for train quiet zones
hero.teaser: A 10:30 a.m. presentation Tuesday will examine potential quiet-zone benefits, risks and crossing improvements following continued pressure from residents.
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners are scheduled to review safety requirements and potential improvements Tuesday morning for proposed railroad quiet zones, which would end routine train horn requirements at designated crossings. The review follows continued pressure from residents seeking relief from train noise along the Florida East Coast Railway.

 Public Works staff is scheduled to present an update at 10:30 a.m. on the Railroad Safety Capital Improvement Program and the county’s evaluation of establishing one or more quiet zones. The presentation will outline potential risks and benefits, along with the safety requirements and improvements needed to establish the zones. Commissioners are expected to discuss the findings and give staff direction on how to proceed.

 Crossings would have to meet federal safety requirements before quiet zones could be established. Train engineers would retain the ability to sound their horns when necessary for safety. Hobe Sound resident Glenn Malone supports reducing horn noise while preserving engineers’ ability to use the horn for safety. Another Hobe Sound resident, Jeffry Aderman, has raised concerns about train noise throughout the day and night.

 Brightline began commercial operations along the Florida East Coast Railway through the Treasure Coast in September 2023, adding approximately 32 daily train trips through the corridor. The increased rail traffic prompted residents to call on county leaders to explore quiet zones.

 Commissioners decided against pursuing quiet zones at a March 11, 2025, meeting after reviewing options presented by county staff. Following continued resident concerns, they revisited the issue in May 2026 and directed staff to continue evaluating the possibility. Tuesday’s scheduled presentation continues that evaluation.

hero.headline: Western St. Lucie County flooding prompts emergency meeting, push for faster study
hero.teaser: The North St. Lucie River Water Control District held an emergency meeting Monday after last week’s flooding submerged homes, farms and roads in western St. Lucie County. Later Mon
hero.body:
The North St. Lucie River Water Control District held an emergency meeting Monday after last week’s flooding submerged homes, farms and roads in western St. Lucie County. Later Monday, Port St. Lucie Councilman David Pickett urged the city to accelerate a stormwater study planned for 2029.

 Farmers, residents and representatives of Save the Chimps attended the district meeting to seek answers and long-term drainage solutions. District President Steve Cassens said the existing system has limits during extreme rainfall. “We can manage water maybe 3, 4, 5, 6 inches. We can’t manage water in the quantities that we got.” District officials discussed examining engineering options as part of a possible long-range plan.

 They also addressed waterway and ditch maintenance, including concerns about a creek in Western Fort Pierce that serves as a primary drainage route. The district said it systematically cleans ditches within its boundaries.

 At Monday’s Port St. Lucie City Council meeting, Pickett said he had sent two memos to the city manager addressing floodwaters and wanted the stormwater study expedited rather than waiting until 2029. He also raised concerns about flooding in Tradition and called for examining stormwater systems before distributing certain stormwater fees to community development districts.

 Justin Akerley, who helps operate Saint Lucie Farm Preserve in west Fort Pierce, attended both meetings. He told council members he believes continued development is adding pressure to drainage infrastructure and urged city leaders to reconsider development’s effects on flooding. “I’ve got friends that have calves dying that are flooded, they can’t get out,” he said. “It’s a terrible, terrible situation for everybody.

 There’s people that have lost their homes.” Akerley and Michael Hale operate the working agritourism farm, which produces hay, cut flowers, beef and assorted vegetables. The farm also hosts community agricultural events.

 Conditions had significantly improved at Save the Chimps, a sanctuary in western St. Lucie County where staff used drones to deliver food to chimpanzees while several roads were underwater. “A short 40 hours after that, we’re almost completely dry on our roads,” Mark Yohannan said. Residents and farmers at Monday’s district meeting sought ways to reduce the risk of similar flooding during another extreme rainfall event.

hero.headline: SUV turned into motorcycle’s path in fatal Indian River County crash, FHP says
hero.teaser: The Florida Highway Patrol says an SUV turned left into the path of a motorcycle during Monday’s fatal crash on 37th Street. The motorcyclist, a 58-year-old man, died at a hospital, and the SUV driver suffered minor injuries.
hero.body:
A crash Monday afternoon on 37th Street in Indian River County initially reported as killing at least one person involved an SUV turning into a motorcycle’s path, according to new details from the Florida Highway Patrol. FHP said the motorcycle’s 58-year-old driver died after being taken to a hospital, while the SUV driver suffered minor injuries.

 The collision occurred around 3:43 p.m. near 1850 37th Street in unincorporated Indian River County. According to FHP, an 82-year-old woman was driving a 2018 Toyota RAV4 east on 37th Street before the crash. She stopped in the roadway while waiting to make a left turn into Indian River MRI.

 The SUV then turned into the path of a westbound 2017 Harley-Davidson motorcycle, and the two vehicles collided, FHP said. The agency’s account provides details about the vehicles involved and their movements before the collision that were not included in the initial report of the fatal crash.

 The motorcycle driver was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where he was pronounced dead. FHP reported that the woman driving the SUV had minor injuries. The initial report had not specified who died or provided information about injuries to the other driver.

 The crash prompted the closure of westbound 37th Street between U.S. Highway 1 and 17th Avenue. The Florida Highway Patrol described its investigation into the fatal collision as active.

cards.headline: Florida's Roof Age Law: The Roof Inspection Treasure Coast Homeowners Can Request Before Replacing a Roof Over 15 Years Old
cards.teaser: Under Florida Statute 627.7011, a homeowner with a roof 15 years or older can have it inspected before an insurer requires replacement. Here is what Martin and St. Lucie County homeowners should know, and what a proper roof inspection documents.
cards.body:
If you own a home in Stuart, Jensen Beach, Palm City, Port St. Lucie, Fort Pierce or anywhere along Hutchinson Island, and your roof is more than 15 years old, there is a good chance you have already received the letter. It says your homeowners insurance will not be renewed unless the roof is replaced. Many Treasure Coast homeowners assume they have two choices: pay for a new roof or lose coverage. Florida law gives them a third option, and most have never heard of it.

 What Florida's Roof Age Law Actually Says

 Florida Statute 627.7011(5), often called the Florida roof age law or the 15-year roof rule, applies to homeowners insurance policies issued or renewed on or after July 1, 2022. For a roof under 15 years old, an insurer may not refuse to issue or renew a policy solely because of the roof's age. For a roof 15 years or older, the insurer must allow the homeowner to have the roof inspected by an authorized inspector, at the homeowner's expense, before requiring replacement as a condition of coverage. If that roof inspection shows the roof has five or more years of remaining useful life, the insurer may not refuse to issue or renew the policy solely because of roof age.

 Authorized inspectors under the statute include Florida-licensed roofing contractors, home inspectors, building code inspectors, general or residential contractors, engineers and architects. The law applies to homeowners policies; it does not apply to a condominium association's master policy, and it does not override every other underwriting decision a carrier is allowed to make. It is a right to be inspected on the roof's actual condition rather than its birthday.

 A plain-language summary of the statute, with the text of the law, is available on our Florida roof age law resource page at mmroofrepair.com/florida-roof-age-law.

 Why Roof Age and Roof Condition Are Not the Same Thing

 On the Treasure Coast, most older homes carry concrete or clay tile roofs. Tile is not the waterproofing layer. The underlayment beneath the tile is.

 A 20- or 25-year-old tile roof can have tile that is largely sound and underlayment that still has service life, with failures concentrated in the places that handle the most water: valleys, perimeter edges, and flashing transitions around chimneys, walls and skylights. Those are the areas that age fastest, because that is where the water goes.

 That is why a documented tile roof inspection so often tells a different story than the installation date. In the more than 100 five-year roof certifications our company has issued since 2023, the deficiencies that put an older tile roof at risk have usually been localized and repairable, not spread evenly across the entire roof. Earlier this year we certified a 25-year-old oceanfront tile roof in Highland Beach that, by age alone, would have been scheduled for a full tear-off.

 The valleys and perimeter edges were rebuilt with new self-adhered underlayment and copper drip edge, each tile went back in its original position, and the roof was certified for more than five years of remaining life with a ten-page photographic record .

 What a Proper Roof Inspection and Five-Year Roof Certification Should Document

 Not every piece of paper called a roof certification is worth the same. A credible five-year roof certification is a licensed professional's written opinion, based on an actual inspection, and it should contain five parts:

 Findings: what the inspector observed across each roof system, including tile, flat sections, underlayment where sampled, flashing and penetrations. Deficiencies identified: active leaks, broken or loose tiles, deteriorated underlayment, damaged sheathing and flashing failures, recorded by location. Repairs performed: exactly what was corrected before the certification was signed. Remaining useful life opinion: the inspector's professional judgment, stated with its basis. Limitations: what was not inspected or tested. A certification is not a warranty, and an honest one says so. Every finding should be tied to dated photographs and the inspector's license number. If a document cannot show you where the problem was found and how it was addressed, it is an opinion without evidence, and it will not hold up when it matters.

 What to Do When the Non-Renewal Letter Arrives

 Read the letter carefully and note the deadline. Most give a defined window to respond. Ask your agent, in writing, whether the non-renewal is based on roof age, and reference Florida Statute 627.7011(5). Schedule a roof inspection with an authorized inspector, and ask up front what the written report will include and whether the inspector photographs every deficiency. If repairs are needed to reach five years of remaining life, have them completed and documented before the certification is signed. Deliver the inspection report and certification to your agent, and keep a copy with your closing documents and your wind mitigation report. Five Questions to Ask Before Signing a Roof Replacement Contract

 Has anyone inspected and photographed the roof's actual condition, or is replacement being recommended by age alone? Where exactly is the roof failing, and is the failure localized to valleys, edges and flashings, or spread across the field? Can the failing sections be rebuilt with new underlayment while the existing tile is preserved and reinstalled? Is the contractor a Florida-licensed roofing contractor, and is the license number on the proposal? Will the contractor return for annual roof inspections so the documentation stays current? When Roof Replacement Is the Right Answer

 This is not an argument against replacing roofs. Some roofs are at the end of their service life. When underlayment has failed across the field, when sheathing is deteriorated in many areas, or when the tile itself is no longer serviceable, replacement is the responsible decision and a good contractor will say so.

 The concern is the roof that gets torn off because of a date on a permit, before anyone has inspected, documented and explained its actual condition. Florida law gives homeowners the right to that inspection. The homeowners who benefit are the ones who know to ask for it.
